lesson.title: Practical Domain: Letting the Real World Prune the Algebra
lesson.summary: Every applied optimization problem inherits a domain from its physical setup, not just from the algebra. Use a printed poster problem to see a negative algebraic root get discarded on physical grounds before calculus even runs.
lesson.body:
Pure algebra treats x^2 = 25 as having two solutions, x = 5 and x = -5. Applied optimization problems almost never allow both, because the variable x usually stands for something physical, a length, a count of items, a price, and that physical meaning restricts the domain before any derivative is even taken. Recognizing the practical domain early, directly from the problem's setup rather than from the algebra, is what separates a correct applied answer from a technically correct but physically meaningless one.

Consider a poster that must contain exactly 50 square inches of printed material. The poster needs 4 inch margins at the top and bottom and 2 inch margins on each side. The goal is to minimize the total area of the poster, printed material plus all its margins.

Let x be the width of the printed material and y be its height, so xy = 50, meaning y = 50/x. The total width of the poster, printed material plus its two 2 inch side margins, is x + 4. The total height, printed material plus its 4 inch top and bottom margins, is y + 8. The total poster area is A(x) = (x + 4)(50/x + 8).

Expand this: A(x) = 50 + 8x + 200/x + 32 = 8x + 200/x + 82. Differentiate: A'(x) = 8 - 200/x^2. Setting this to zero gives x^2 = 25, so algebraically x = 5 or x = -5. This is exactly where the practical domain matters. The variable x represents the width of printed material on an actual poster, and a width cannot be negative, so x = -5 is discarded immediately, not because of any derivative test, but simply because it is physically impossible. Only x = 5 survives as a candidate, and this pruning happens before the second derivative test is even needed.

Verify x = 5 with the second derivative: A''(x) = 400/x^3, and A''(5) = 400/125 = 3.2, which is positive, confirming a minimum. With x = 5, y = 50/5 = 10, so the total poster dimensions are width 5 + 4 = 9 inches and height 10 + 8 = 18 inches, giving a total minimum area of 9 times 18 = 162 square inches. This matches plugging x = 5 directly into A(x) = 8x + 200/x + 82 = 40 + 40 + 82 = 162.

Notice the shape of this domain compared to earlier problems in this unit. Here the practical domain is simply x > 0, with no finite upper limit at all, unlike the box problem's domain of 0 < x < 6 or the fencing problem's domain of 0 < x < 800/3, both of which had a ceiling imposed by the geometry as well as a floor. As x approaches 0, the printed material becomes an impossibly thin sliver and A(x) grows without bound; as x grows very large, the poster becomes impossibly wide and A(x) grows without bound again. Because both ends of this open domain push the area toward infinity, the single interior critical point at x = 5 is guaranteed to be the global minimum, with no endpoint comparison required, since there are no finite endpoints to compare against in the first place.

The habit worth building here is to ask, before differentiating anything, exactly what values the variable is allowed to take in the real situation it represents. Must it be strictly positive? Is there a finite upper bound coming from the geometry, or does the domain stretch out to infinity in one or both directions? That practical domain determines which algebraic solutions are worth keeping, and whether the endpoint checking method from the previous chapter will even be needed at all.
